extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (PR students, PR educators, PR counselors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the major models of public relations practice (press agentry, public-information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric), historical examples, and when to use each model; includes practical rules for press releases/handouts and counsel responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agentry/publicity model
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-way model focused on gaining publicity and attention (high-pressure methods, advertising, news planting). Historically used for sensational promotion and to publicize events or personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the primary objective is to generate publicity (example: sell tickets to a baseball game). Methods may include staged events, press agentry and planting stories; recognized as one-way and not aimed at mutual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-information model
rubrics_metrics.description: One-way dissemination of accurate, complete information to the public—informing rather than overtly persuading. Practitioners act like 'journalists in residence' providing factual material to the press and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for organizations (especially government agencies constrained by law) whose role is to provide information (example: government health information). Emphasizes openness, frankness, and candid disclosure rather than propaganda (Arthur Page: 'candid disclosure rather than parochial propaganda').

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release / handout best practice (Ivy Lee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handouts (press releases) should be clearly marked to indicate who wrote them and on whose behalf; avoid anonymous planted tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ivy Lee rehabilitated the handout by making them 'respectable'—his handouts 'were always clearly marked to indicate who wrote them, and on whose behalf.' Anti-pattern: planting anonymous handouts or leaking anonymous tips, which undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the PR counsel (interpretation and advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations practitioner interprets the organization to the public and the public to the organization (counsel on public relations). Advises management when policies might conflict with public opinion and helps shape management policy in discussion stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel acts like a lawyer in the court of public opinion—representing the client's interests 'as far as public opinion will permit.' Also expected to serve as a 'listening post' for management, warning when actions may provoke adverse public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way asymmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-way model that uses social science and research to learn about publics and then crafts persuasive messages to influence them; communication is used to benefit the client by shaping publics' views and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practiced by Edward Bernays and others: use opinion polls, segmental approaches, and psychological principles to discover 'what the public liked' or 'what values and attitudes publics had' and then present the organization in line with those. Appropriate for marketing products or influencing legislation. Limitation: often tells management what the public will accept rather than advising management to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way symmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: A model emphasizing dialogue, mutual understanding, and adjustment between organization and publics; PR serves to harmonize interests and to help management adapt to social trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners and educators describe the counsel's role as both interpreting publics to the client and helping mold client actions. Appropriate for large, regulated firms or when the objective is maintaining social responsibility. Goal shifts from persuasion to understanding and mutual adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency view for choosing PR model
rubrics_metrics.description: No single PR model is best for all situations; the appropriate model depends on the nature of the organization, its technology, its environment, and the specific problem or objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative mappings given: selling event tickets → press agentry/publicity; government health dissemination → public-information model; marketing/product or legislative influence → two-way asymmetric; large regulated firms maintaining social responsibility → two-way symmetric. Practitioners should select the model that fits the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social science and research in PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing scientific opinion polls, surveys, and social-psychological insights to learn what publics believe and will accept; moves PR from intuition toward research-based program direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polling and research 'give an organization the ability to learn what the public wants and will accept, thus indicating the direction a public relations program should take.' Bernays used informal surveys and later social science concepts (e.g., 'segmental approach'); the development of scientific polling in the 1940s–50s made the two-way asymmetric model more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical tension: serving client vs. public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners claim to protect public and social welfare but may also use PR to advance client interests; historical criticism exists that some practitioners 'whitewashed' clients or represented despised clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the ethical tension: Lee advised openness yet was criticized (called 'Poison Ivy'); Bernays advocated public welfare while engineering consent. Practitioners must be aware of potential conflicts between promoting client interests and defending the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government constraints (Gillett Amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal law (Gillett Amendment, 1913) prohibits government agencies from hiring 'publicity experts' unless money is specifically appropriated; limits government to providing information rather than practicing publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, government agencies are 'essentially limited to practicing the public-information model.' Practitioners working with government must respect statutory limits and emphasize informational rather than promotional activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthur Page / corporate disclosure principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Business should be willing to tell the public what its policies are, what it is doing, and what it hopes to do; public relations as duty to maintain public permission and approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page's philosophy supports candid disclosure as a corporate duty: 'All business in a democratic country begins with public permission and exists by public approval.' Use candid disclosure to build trust; combined with opinion research, this can move a firm toward two-way practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallizing public opinion / engineering of consent (Bernays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategy of identifying what publics already believe or value and then shaping messages and presentations that crystallize those opinions to achieve client goals ('crystallizing of public opinion' and the 'engineering of consent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include appealing to existing sympathies or segmenting audiences by interest, then stimulating action (e.g., letters to congressmen). Useful for creating acceptance of products or policies when there is a 'coincidence of interest' between public and private aims.
